gloss: To experience something from the past again, usually in memory or imagination.
examples: Veterans often *relive* the same night in their dreams.
She *relived* the crash every time she drove past that corner.
He has been *reliving* his college years all week.
contrast: Not *relieve* /rɪˈliːv/ (ri-LEEV), which means to take pain or pressure away.

ru: возвращать (дело) на новое рассмотрение; заключать под стражу
gloss: To send a case back to a lower court, or to send a defendant back into custody.
examples: Appeals courts often *remand* cases for a new hearing.
The judge *remanded* him to county jail without bail.
The lawsuit was *remanded* to state court last month.

gloss: To produce a new, better-quality version of a recording or film from the original source.
examples: The studio plans to *remaster* the whole trilogy in 4K.
They *remastered* the album from the original tapes.
A *remastered* version streams next week.

gloss: To clean up contamination or fix a serious problem in a place or a program.
examples: The state will pay to *remediate* the contaminated soil.
The district *remediated* the lead problem over the summer.
Crews are *remediating* mold in three schools.

transitivity: both — transitive (*remit the balance*), intransitive (*please remit by Friday*)
gloss: To send money in payment to a person or office at a distance.
examples: Workers abroad *remit* billions of dollars to their families every year.
The company *remitted* the sales tax to the state.
Payment must be *remitted* within thirty days.
contrast: The t doubles before an ending: *remit → remitted → remitting*.

gloss: To protest or argue forcefully with someone about something you think is wrong.
examples: Parents came to *remonstrate* with the principal about the new rules.
He *remonstrated* loudly, but the referee waved him away.
She stood at the counter *remonstrating* with the clerk for ten minutes.
contrast: You *remonstrate with* a person *about* or *over* a thing.

gloss: To pay someone for work they have done or costs they have carried.
examples: Good firms *remunerate* their staff fairly.
Panel members were *remunerated* for each day of hearings.
The lab is *remunerating* volunteers out of grant money.
contrast: Note the order of the letters: re-MU-ne-rate, not "renumerate" — that spelling is simply wrong.

gloss: To meet someone at an arranged place and time.
examples: The two boats *rendezvous* at dawn off the coast.
We *rendezvoused* with the guide at the trailhead.
The capsule is *rendezvousing* with the station tonight.
contrast: The final s is silent: RAHN-day-voo, past RAHN-day-vood. Only the third-person *rendezvouses* has a spoken -z (RAHN-day-vooz).

gloss: To break a promise or go back on an agreement.
examples: Politicians who *renege* on their promises lose voters fast.
The buyer *reneged* on the deal a week before closing.
They accused the city of *reneging* on the contract.
contrast: Always *renege on* something. The final e drops before -ing: *renege → reneging*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*renegotiate the contract*), intransitive (*renegotiate with the lender*)
gloss: To discuss an existing agreement again in order to change its terms.
examples: The team wants to *renegotiate* his contract before the season starts.
We *renegotiated* the loan at a lower rate.
The treaty is being *renegotiated* in Geneva.

transitivity: both — transitive (*reorder the filters*), intransitive (*we reorder every month*)
gloss: To order a supply of something again, or to arrange things in a different sequence.
examples: Call the supplier and *reorder* the filters.
She *reordered* the slides so the chart came first.
We have been *reordering* the same part every spring.

transitivity: both — transitive (*reorient the strategy*), intransitive (*reorient after a long flight*)
gloss: To turn something, or yourself, in a new direction or toward a new purpose.
examples: The company plans to *reorient* itself toward electric vehicles.
After the layoffs he *reoriented* his career around teaching.
They are *reorienting* the whole program around online classes.

ru: переупаковывать, переупаковать; подавать в новом виде
gloss: To put something in new packaging, or to present an old idea in a new form.
examples: Stores often *repackage* returned goods before selling them again.
The senator simply *repackaged* an old proposal with a new name.
The show is being *repackaged* for a younger audience.

gloss: To send a person, money, or object back to the country it came from.
examples: The museum agreed to *repatriate* the looted artifacts.
Thousands of workers were *repatriated* after the border closed.
The company is *repatriating* profits held overseas.

transitivity: both — intransitive (*he repented of his lies*), transitive (*she repented her decision*)
gloss: To feel deep regret for something you have done wrong.
examples: The preacher urged the crowd to *repent*.
He *repented* of the way he had treated his family.
She has never *repented* a single word of it.
contrast: In the intransitive use it takes *of*: *repent of your mistakes*.

gloss: To take back goods from a buyer who has not kept up the payments.
examples: Lenders can *repossess* a car after three missed payments.
The bank *repossessed* their house last spring.
He worked two jobs to keep the truck from being *repossessed*.

gloss: To move something into a different position, or to present a product or person in a new way.
examples: The nurse helped him *reposition* the pillow.
The brand *repositioned* itself as a budget option.
They are *repositioning* the satellite dish for a better signal.

gloss: To move a plant into a different, usually larger, pot.
examples: *Repot* the seedlings once they have four leaves.
She *repotted* the fern in something bigger.
Most houseplants need to be *repotted* every couple of years.
contrast: The t doubles before an ending: *repot → repotted → repotting*.

gloss: To hold back a feeling or an impulse, or to put down opposition by force.
examples: He tried to *repress* a smile during the speech.
The regime *repressed* every attempt to protest.
Those memories had been *repressed* for years.

gloss: To cancel or delay a punishment, or to save something from being shut down.
examples: Only the governor can *reprieve* a condemned prisoner.
The court *reprieved* him three hours before the execution.
The neighborhood library has been *reprieved* for another year.

gloss: To perform or take on a role, song, or part again.
examples: She will *reprise* her role in the sequel.
The band *reprised* the chorus one last time.
He is *reprising* the part he played on Broadway.
contrast: Say ri-PREEZ, not "ri-PRYZ". The noun *reprisal* (revenge) is a different word: /rɪˈpraɪzəl/.

gloss: To give a machine, or a habit of mind, a new set of instructions.
examples: You can *reprogram* the thermostat from your phone.
The dealer *reprogrammed* the key fob in ten minutes.
Therapy is partly about *reprogramming* old reactions.
contrast: The m doubles: *reprogrammed*, *reprogramming* — the single-m spellings are rare in American writing.

gloss: To reject something publicly and completely, refusing to accept or be bound by it.
examples: Party leaders were quick to *repudiate* the remarks.
He *repudiated* the confession as soon as he had a lawyer.
The country has *repudiated* its foreign debt twice.

gloss: To drive back an attack, or to fill someone with disgust.
examples: Fresh troops helped *repulse* the attack.
The smell of the kitchen *repulsed* her.
Voters were *repulsed* by the tone of the ads.
contrast: Two senses: *repulse an attack* = push it back; *be repulsed by* something = be disgusted by it.

gloss: To use something for a purpose other than the one it was made for.
examples: The city wants to *repurpose* the old mill as apartments.
She *repurposed* an old door as a desktop.
They are *repurposing* the footage for a documentary.

gloss: To demand or order supplies through an official request, especially by an army or an agency.
examples: Units can *requisition* extra fuel through headquarters.
The army *requisitioned* every truck in the village.
New laptops have been *requisitioned* for the whole department.

gloss: To send traffic, a flight, or a delivery along a different route.
examples: Crews had to *reroute* traffic around the sinkhole.
The storm *rerouted* dozens of flights to Denver.
Buses are being *rerouted* through downtown all week.
contrast: Americans say either ree-ROOT or ree-ROWT; both are accepted.

gloss: To rearrange people or things into a different order or set of jobs.
examples: The coach may *reshuffle* the lineup before the playoffs.
The governor *reshuffled* her cabinet after the election.
Management is *reshuffling* the whole department again.

gloss: To live in a particular place, or, of a power or quality, to belong to someone.
examples: Roughly eight million people *reside* in the metro area.
She *resided* in Ohio for most of her adult life.
Students *residing* on campus must register their cars.
contrast: Formal. In everyday speech Americans say *live*. Power *resides in* or *with* a body: *authority resides with the board*.

gloss: To turn to something unpleasant or extreme because nothing else has worked.
examples: Don't *resort* to threats when a phone call would do.
The city *resorted* to rationing water in August.
He won the seat without ever *resorting* to negative ads.
contrast: Always *resort to*. The noun *resort* (a vacation hotel) is spelled the same but is a separate sense.

gloss: To fill a place with loud sound, or to echo off its walls.
examples: Cheers *resound* through the arena after every goal.
The gunshot *resounded* across the valley.
The hall was *resounding* with applause.
contrast: The -ing form doubles as an adjective meaning 'emphatic': *a resounding success*.

gloss: To happen as the effect of something, or to have something as an effect.
examples: Long hours often *result* in careless mistakes.
The fire *resulted* from a faulty space heater.
Two flights were canceled, *resulting* in long lines at the counter.
contrast: Opposite directions: *result in* names the outcome (*the crash resulted in delays*); *result from* names the cause (*the delays resulted from the crash*).

transitivity: both — intransitive (*the rumor resurfaced*), transitive (*resurface the road*)
gloss: To appear again after a long absence, or to put a new surface on something.
examples: Old rumors *resurface* every election year.
The video *resurfaced* years after it was filmed.
Crews are *resurfacing* the parking lot this week.

transitivity: both — transitive (*they retail furniture*), intransitive (*it retails for $40*)
gloss: To sell goods to the public, or, of an item, to be sold at a stated price.
examples: The sneakers *retail* for about ninety dollars.
The chain *retailed* its own brand of coffee for years.
They are *retailing* the same product under a new name.
contrast: Stress falls on the first syllable: REE-tayl.

gloss: To slow down the growth, progress, or spread of something.
examples: Shade *retards* the ripening of the fruit.
The coating *retarded* the spread of the flames.
Engineers added a layer of foam, *retarding* the heat for crucial minutes.
contrast: Technical and formal only. Applied to a person, the related adjective is a serious insult in American English — in everyday speech say *slow down* or *delay*.

ru: тужиться при рвоте, давиться рвотными позывами
gloss: To make the motions and sounds of vomiting, with or without bringing anything up.
examples: The smell alone made him *retch*.
She *retched* twice before the medicine took effect.
He knelt by the sink, *retching* and shaking.
contrast: A homophone of *wretch* (a pitiable person), and not the same as *reach* /riːtʃ/.

transitivity: both — transitive (*retool the factory*), intransitive (*the plant retooled for masks*)
gloss: To re-equip a factory for new production, or to rebuild a plan or program for a new purpose.
examples: The plant will *retool* to build electric motors.
They *retooled* the whole ad campaign after the launch flopped.
The company is *retooling* its factories in Ohio.

transitivity: both — transitive (*he retorted that it was a lie*), intransitive (*she retorted sharply*)
gloss: To answer back quickly and sharply, especially to a criticism.
examples: Don't *retort* every time someone criticizes your work.
"I never said that," he *retorted*.
The senator has *retorted* that the report is politically motivated.

ru: возвращаться по своим следам; восстанавливать (ход событий)
gloss: To go back over a route or a sequence of events in order to find something or understand it.
examples: If you lose your keys, *retrace* your steps.
Detectives *retraced* the victim's last evening hour by hour.
We spent the morning *retracing* the route on the map.

ru: сокращать расходы, урезать; отступать (с прежних позиций)
transitivity: both — intransitive (*the firm retrenched*), transitive (*retrench spending*)
gloss: To cut spending or pull back from commitments in order to survive harder times.
examples: When sales fall, small firms *retrench* fast.
The university *retrenched* after donations dried up.
Washington has been *retrenching* from commitments abroad.

gloss: To try a case in court a second time, or to attempt an action again.
examples: Prosecutors may *retry* the case in the fall.
The state *retried* him after the first jury deadlocked.
The app keeps *retrying* the connection.
contrast: The y changes to i: *retry → retries → retried*, but stays in *retrying*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*reunify families*), intransitive (*the country reunified*)
gloss: To bring a divided country, group, or family back together.
examples: The agency's job is to *reunify* children with their parents.
Germany *reunified* in 1990.
Hundreds of families have been *reunified* since the ruling.
contrast: The y changes to i: *reunify → reunifies → reunified*, but stays in *reunifying*.

gloss: To echo loudly through a space, or to have effects that spread far beyond the event.
examples: Low notes *reverberate* through the whole building.
The verdict *reverberated* across the industry.
The blast was still *reverberating* when the alarms started.

gloss: To feel deep respect and admiration for someone or something.
examples: Many players still *revere* their old coach.
Critics *revered* her early films.
He is *revered* as the founder of modern jazz.

gloss: To take great, open pleasure in something.
examples: Some coaches *revel* in the pressure of a big game.
She *reveled* in the attention for a week.
He spent the afternoon *reveling* in his win.
contrast: Takes *in*. American spelling keeps one l — *reveled*, *reveling*; British writes *revelled*, *revelling*.

gloss: To criticize someone with hatred and contempt.
examples: Columnists *revile* him one week and quote him the next.
Fans *reviled* the trade for years afterward.
The law was *reviled* by both parties.

gloss: To change something so completely that it works in an entirely new way.
examples: Cheap sensors could *revolutionize* farming.
The smartphone *revolutionized* the way we take pictures.
New drugs are *revolutionizing* cancer treatment.
contrast: American spelling uses -ize; British writes *revolutionise*.

gloss: To put new electrical wiring in a building or device, or to change deeply fixed habits of thinking.
examples: An electrician will have to *rewire* the whole basement.
They *rewired* the house before moving in.
Meditation may be slowly *rewiring* how he reacts to stress.

gloss: To tease someone in a friendly way.
examples: His friends still *rib* him about that haircut.
The crew *ribbed* the new guy all morning.
She was only *ribbing* you.
contrast: Informal, and the b doubles: *rib → ribbed → ribbing*.

gloss: To bounce off a hard surface and fly away at an angle.
examples: Bullets *ricochet* off the steel plates.
The puck *ricocheted* into the net off a defender's skate.
Rocks came *ricocheting* down the slope.
contrast: The final t is silent: RIK-uh-shay, past RIK-uh-shayd.

gloss: To fill something with holes, or with faults and problems.
examples: Rust had begun to *riddle* the old fenders.
Gunfire *riddled* the side of the building.
The report was *riddled* with errors.
contrast: Usually in the passive with *with*: *riddled with bullets*, *riddled with debt*.
